metadata.note: Yes -- the line Amtrak's Pere Marquette uses to reach Chicago from Grand Rapids today is the same historical corridor, built in stages between 1870 and 1903. The Chicago and Michigan Lake Shore Railroad opened the first piece (St. Joseph-Union Pier) Feb 2 1870, extended north to Grand Rapids by 1871-72, and its successor the Pere Marquette Railway (formed 1900, see michigan_central_lansing_saginaw.geojson for the other 1900 Pere Marquette merger components) completed the southern extension from Union Pier to Porter, Indiana in 1903 -- finally linking Grand Rapids through to the Chicago rail network via the same Porter/Kensington gateway the Michigan Central used (see michigan_central_detroit_chicago.geojson). Pere Marquette merged into the Chesapeake & Ohio in 1947, extending through service to Chicago itself. Amtrak revived the Pere Marquette name for this exact route on August 5 1984, and still runs it today (see amtrak.geojson). Geometry is real-traced from OpenStreetMap active-rail geometry for nearly the whole route -- only the final ~15km approach into downtown Chicago (dense terminal trackage, the same gap that shows up on the other lines converging there) is a straight-line approximation.

geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API), railway=rail ways tagged usage=main, for the Grand Rapids-Holland-Bangor-St.Joseph-New Buffalo-Porter-Kensington corridor -- still active track today as Amtrak's Pere Marquette route
metadata.chicago_terminal_note: Chicago end truncated Aug 2026. The trace previously ran past its terminal, doubled back south down the ex-Illinois Central main line to 71st Street, then jumped 9 km further south and 18 km back north to a downtown-Chicago anchor point that lay on no track at all. It now ends where the route reaches the ex-Illinois Central main at 18th Street -- the approach to Central Station, the Michigan Central's Chicago passenger terminal from 1893. Note the Chicago approach still contains straight-line chords of about 7.8 km and 5.0 km where the trace is incomplete, and follows the modern NS Chicago Line alignment rather than the historic Michigan Central/Illinois Central route in from Kensington.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
